HomeStyle Retail - Q2 Fiscal 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeStyle Retail Q2 Fiscal 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeStyle Retail's results for the second quarter of fiscal 2024. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and David Patel, Chief Merchandising Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeStyle Retail's performance for Q2 fiscal 2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover five key aspects of our performance, starting with our overall results. We posted total net sales of $4.8 billion, reflecting a 5.2 percent increase year over year and surpassing our guidance midpoint as well as consensus estimates by 150 basis points. This marked our eighth straight quarter of sales growth in a tough retail landscape with ongoing inflation, weaker consumer confidence, and higher interest rates, much like what peers such as Home Depot and Lowe's have navigated recently. Comparable store sales rose 3.8 percent, supported by 2.1 percent higher traffic—our best in more than a year—and a 1.6 percent increase in average basket size to $128. Average unit retail climbed 2.4 percent as shoppers moved toward premium options, including energy-efficient appliances amid climbing utility bills.

By category, hardlines like tools, lumber, and paint comped up 6.1 percent on strong DIY demand and favorable weather for outdoor work. Appliances jumped 4.9 percent, beating industry averages per Circana data, thanks to solid performance in mid-range smart refrigerators and our exclusive private-label EnergyStar products, which hold 28 percent share in that space. Softlines such as decor and bedding saw a milder 1.2 percent comp increase due to lingering inflation in related areas, though refreshed seasonal collections showed promising early momentum.

Gross margins improved 110 basis points to 32.4 percent, the strongest Q2 since 2019, thanks to enhanced inventory productivity with turns at 5.2 times versus 4.8 times, efficiencies from our consolidated West Coast distribution center, and less reliance on heavy promotions. Shrink control added 60 basis points through AI shelf-scanning in 250 stores, cutting out-of-stocks by 15 percent and losses by 22 percent. Adjusted EBITDA rose 12.4 percent to $620 million, expanding margins 90 basis points to 12.9 percent, while SG&A deleveraged 40 basis points to 19.2 percent of sales via optimized labor scheduling with Kronos tools and favorable lease terms. Diluted EPS reached $1.42, up 18 percent and topping our $1.35 guidance, despite a $15 million tariff hit on imported cabinetry.

Geographically, the Sunbelt—including Florida, Texas, and the Carolinas—led with 5.6 percent comps from population shifts, home sales, and 12 new stores in growth areas like Austin and Phoenix, already positive on a two-year basis. Midwest comps were steady at 3.2 percent on agriculture strength, Northeast at 1.9 percent hampered by wet weather and big-ticket caution, similar to Target's notes. Our 45 Canadian stores comped 4.1 percent in local currency, aided by bilingual loyalty app uptake. We're emphasizing omnichannel, with BOPIS at 28 percent of digital sales versus 22 percent last year, supported by store micro-fulfillment for two-hour delivery in 80 percent of markets. The HomeStyle Rewards program now has 18 million members, lifting repeat traffic 14 percent with targeted app deals. Tech upgrades like RFID on 40 percent of SKUs by year-end will enhance visibility, much like Walmart's approach, adding 50 basis points to FY25 margins. Our balance sheet is robust with $750 million YTD operating cash flow, net debt to EBITDA at 1.8 times, and $1.2 billion liquidity, while returning $400 million to shareholders through buybacks and a 2.3 percent yielding dividend. This quarter confirms our stores-first, digital-everywhere strategy for value home improvements as housing stabilizes. For Q3, we expect 2.5 to 3.5 percent comps, 4 to 5 percent full-year sales growth, and EBITDA margins over 13 percent.

Next, e-commerce growth, which remains a powerhouse offsetting softer store traffic amid inflation and prudent spending. E-commerce sales surged 25.4 percent year over year to $710 million from $566 million, our 11th straight double-digit quarter, accelerating from 21.7 percent last year and exceeding U.S. retail e-commerce growth of 8 to 10 percent per Census Bureau data. Penetration rose to 14.8 percent of total sales from 12.1 percent, with trailing twelve-month at a record 13.9 percent—upper quartile versus Macy's and Kohl's, closing the gap with pure-plays like Amazon on profits.

Key drivers included traffic up 32 percent to 129 million unique monthly visitors, with mobile app sessions soaring 41 percent to 62 percent of traffic from 55 percent, powered by our Q4 FY23 app overhaul featuring AR virtual room planners for furnishings and decor, akin to Wayfair and IKEA. Conversion climbed to 3.8 percent from 3.2 percent via Adobe Commerce personalization and ML boosting add-to-cart 18 percent. Growth spanned categories, led by home textiles and bedding—28 percent of digital—at 31 percent up, driven by TikTok 'quiet luxury' buzz and private-label Haven Essentials lifting average order value to $145 from $132. Consumer electronics rose 22 percent on Samsung bundles and a 5,000-SKU marketplace with Dyson and Sonos. Apparel grew 19 percent post-inventory fixes, with AI size predictors cutting returns 12 percent to 22 percent.

U.S. sales—95 percent of total—increased 26.8 percent, strongest in Sunbelt for BOPIS at 28 percent of digital, up from 24 percent, offering 2.5 times repeat rates and CAC of $18 versus $32 for shipped orders. U.K. and Canada pilots grew 45 percent to $34 million, managed carefully to limit cross-border shipping at 14 percent of COGS. Investments of $45 million YTD in infrastructure, including an Atlanta micro-fulfillment center with Manhattan WMS, hit 85 percent next-day delivery from 72 percent, trimming fulfillment to 12.5 percent of sales, down 150 basis points, with e-comm gross margins at 42.3 percent, 210 basis points up and near store levels. Headless commerce on Shopify Plus backend scaled like Target's post-2022 setup. Incrementality shows 78 percent new demand, aiding total comps to 2.1 percent despite flat stores. Q3 guide is 22 to 25 percent growth, full-year penetration 15.5 percent, mindful of textile tariffs (35 percent mix) and parcel hikes, hedged by regional DCs and Zipline drones. LTV/CAC rose to 4.2 times via Omni Rewards at 35 percent of sales, positioning us for 25 percent e-comm penetration by 2027 per McKinsey in a $1.1 trillion market.

Turning to store performance, a critical metric is inventory turnover ratio, or COGS divided by average inventory, measuring sales velocity, carrying costs, and markdown exposure in our store-heavy model amid 15 to 20 percent freight inflation. Full-year FY23 turnover hit 4.2 times, up 80 basis points from 3.9 times and best since 2019; Q4 alone was 4.5 times, topping our 4.3 times goal, equating to 87 days inventory outstanding from 94 days, unlocking $180 million working capital.

By category, apparel/softlines reached 6.8 times from 6.1 times via Fast Fashion Forward, quick-turn on denim/activewear with Levi's/Nike VMI despite 12 percent cotton hikes. Hardlines/home at 3.9 times from 3.4 times, furniture 2.4 times, rightsized amid 19 percent home sales drop per NAR by dropping 15 percent slow SKUs for modular store-ship options. Electronics/seasonal excelled at 7.2 times on BF promotions and Samsung/Apple dropship to 1,200 stores.

Regionally, Northeast/Midwest averaged 4.7 times with stable traffic and Chicago/Boston DC automation 20 percent faster. Southeast 4.1 times despite Hurricane Idalia, aided by Atlanta/Miami MFCs. West Coast 3.8 times on LA port issues, offset by San Francisco RFID pilot lifting 25 percent. Gains from $45 million FY23 tech: Manhattan WMS on 85 percent DCs cutting errors 40 percent; Oracle AI demand sensing at 92 percent accuracy using POS, weather, CPI; RFID to 500 stores slashing shrink 30 bps for daily counts. Omnichannel BOPIS 28 percent digital pulls less store inventory; VMI with P&G/Unilever consignment boosts turns. FY24 guide 4.6 to 4.8 times, sub-85 DIO, markdowns under 25 percent, ahead of Macy's 3.6 times.

On marketing initiatives, we've amplified digital efforts like viral TikTok campaigns for quiet luxury trends, loyalty personalization yielding 35 percent digital sales from members, and exclusive bundles driving electronics growth, all enhancing traffic and conversion across channels.

Finally, supply chain optimization through targeted strategies. In Q3 context but building momentum into Q2, we boosted turnover 22 percent to 5.1 times from 4.2 times, dropping DIO to 71 from 87 days—pre-pandemic levels—expanding gross margins 180 bps to 38.2 percent, markdowns down 15 percent, shrink at 1.2 percent versus peer 1.6 percent. GMROI rose 18 percent to 142 percent, beating Target's 135 percent, freeing $450 million cash for 2.8 times current ratio.

Core tactics: AI demand sensing via RetailFlow on Google Cloud/Manhattan, pulling 50 signals like POS, Placer.ai traffic, Brandwatch sentiment, CPI at 3.7 percent for 91 percent accuracy, cutting overstocks 28 percent—e.g., 35 percent less safety stock in activewear with 98 percent in-stocks, foreseeing Sunbelt heatwaves unlike Kohl's issues. SKU cuts 18 percent to 45,000 A-items (80 percent sales, 60 percent inventory); Assortment Optimizer simulates planograms, localizing for Europe post-Debenhams with more UK outerwear. Omnichannel sync: SFS 28 percent e-comm from stores, RFID 85 percent apparel; 50 MFCs for 22 percent BOPIS same-day, cutting Asia lead times 22 days to 7 amid Red Sea, 97 percent fill rates. VMI with Nike/P&G at 30 percent stock, 96 percent OTIF, forward contracts locking 70 percent Q4 buys; sustainability recycling 25 percent unsold. Store tech: 10,000 Zebra AI cameras for 19 percent fewer OOS, ORC vision holding shrink flat. Regional: Sunbelt hyper-local (Texas grills 6.8 times); Europe inventory down 20 percent private label up; Asia dual-source India. Each 1x turn gain adds 50 bps EBITDA, +8 NPS; FY24 5.8 times target, $600 million FCF, $200 million capex 3x ROI.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for Q2 fiscal 2024.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $4.8 billion, a 5.2 percent increase compared to the same period last year.

Gross margin was 32.4 percent, primarily driven by inventory productivity gains, supply chain efficiencies, and favorable mix shifts.

Operating expenses were $923 million, representing 19.2 percent of revenue.

Net income was $420 million, or $1.42 per share.

We generated $750 million in cash flow from operations year to date.

Inventory levels are currently down 7 percent year over year to $1.45 billion from $1.56 billion, our third straight quarter of declines and lowest since pre-pandemic Q1 2020. On a comp-store basis excluding 12 closures, it's down 8.2 percent, validating our optimization efforts. Apparel (42 percent mix) fell 12 percent to $610 million on 65 percent full-price sell-through in denim/activewear/outerwear versus 58 percent, culling 1,200 low-velocity SKUs like Macy's/Nordstrom Rack, focusing on Levi's/Lululemon. Home goods/decor (28 percent) up 2 percent to $405 million for holidays, with Mexico/Southeast nearshoring trimming lead times to 45 from 65 days. Electronics/hardlines (18 percent) down 9 percent to $260 million, weeks of supply 10.2 from 12.1 despite soft demand like Best Buy. Beauty/wellness (12 percent) flat at $175 million for prestige depth like Estée Lauder/P&G.

Productivity advanced with quarterly turns at 4.1 times from 3.7 times toward full-year 4.0 times goal, DOH 89 from 99 days below NRF 95-day average. Margins stable at 38.2 percent, markdowns under 1 percent via AI forecasting. Sunbelt (55 percent stores) down 11 percent on migration/BOPIS 28 percent; Northeast/Midwest 3 percent drop from weather/inflation, countered by clearances. Tech drivers: Oracle/Blue Yonder real-time sensing, RFID 85 percent apparel for 98 percent accuracy; VMI 22 percent receipts cutting leads 8 days despite Red Sea; Inventory Health Score averting $12 million obsolescence. Lean entering Q4 with 10 percent less stock but 15 percent more holiday heroes, under 2 percent stockouts like Target/Kohl's.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Now, I'd like to hand it over to David Patel, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines.

David Patel, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. This quarter, we launched our Haven Essentials private-label line in home textiles and bedding, which has seen exceptional uptake with 31 percent category growth, higher AOV, and strong cross-sell performance online and in stores. We're excited about the potential of this new product and other upcoming launches in energy-efficient appliances and modular furniture.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of persistent inflation on your sales?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Inflation has indeed pressured consumer sentiment, echoing challenges at peers, but our resilience shines through. Comps held at 3.8 percent with traffic up 2.1 percent and ABS at $128, as shoppers traded up 2.4 percent in AUR to value-driven premiums like EnergyStar appliances amid utility hikes. Softlines comped modestly at 1.2 percent from apparel inflation, but hardlines surged 6.1 percent on DIY. E-comm offset with 25.4 percent growth to $710 million, 78 percent incremental demand. Regionally, Sunbelt strength at 5.6 percent counters Northeast softness. Our Rewards program and BOPIS drove repeats, positioning us well as CPI moderates.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Rodriguez with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Rodriguez (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Emily. For Q3, we're guiding comps to 2.5 to 3.5 percent, balancing macro caution with omnichannel torque. BOPIS at 28 percent digital, micro-fulfillment scaling, and holiday builds in high-velocity items support this, with full-year sales 4 to 5 percent up. Inventory discipline—down 7 percent YoY, turns improving—limits markdowns, aiding margins over 13 percent EBITDA.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Absolutely, David. Our strategies delivered 22 percent turnover gains to 5.1 times, DIO to 71 days via AI RetailFlow sensing at 91 percent accuracy on 50 signals, SKU pruning 18 percent, 50 MFCs for 97 percent fill rates, VMI shifting $300 million risk, and RFID/store AI cutting OOS 19 percent. Nearshoring, forward contracts, and regional clustering like Sunbelt grills de-risked freight/CPI headwinds, freeing $450 million cash while boosting GMROI to 142 percent.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Rachel Kim with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Rachel Kim (Barclays):
How are inventory levels influencing gross margins going forward?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Great question, Rachel. At $1.45 billion, down 7 percent YoY and 8.2 percent comp-store, with turns 4.1 times quarterly, we've minimized markdowns to under 1 percent, holding margins at 38.2 percent. Q4 entry is leaner by 10 percent but optimized for holidays, with Oracle/VMI/RFID ensuring 98 percent accuracy and sub-2 percent stockouts. Expect continued 110 bps expansion drivers into FY25.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session. I'll now turn the call back over to Mike Thompson for closing remarks.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
